newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Perry wants "restrained" arms sales to Latin America.
newsitem.headline: Perry wants "restrained" arms sales to Latin America.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry wants to allow the sale of advanced weaponry to Latin America on a case-by-case basis, but in a "very restrained" fashion to avoid sparking a regional arms race, he said in comments released to reporters on Monday.

Attending a meeting of Western hemisphere defence chiefs in the Argentine Andean resort of Bariloche, Perry said moves to scrap a U.S. ban on high-technology lethal hardware sales to Latin America were still under policy review, but a decision should be made this year.

"Even if we do open it up to case-by-base basis we would still maintain restraint. We would still take every measure to do nothing to stimulate an arms race in the region," said Perry, adding that he agreed with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher "that we need to be very restrained."

U.S. officials attending the meeting of civilian defence chiefs from the United States, Canada and 30 Latin American and Caribbean nations -- Cuba was not invited, Guyana and Haiti dropped out -- say Washington's change of heart on arms sales is in recognition of the region's conversion to democracy.

The United States is particularly eager to help Latin American armed forces modernise their ageing defence systems to help fight drug trafficking and "narco-terrorism" in projects such as operation "Laser Strike", in which it is helping Colombia and Venezuela use radars to catch drug smugglers.

But some Latin Americans are jumpy at the prospect of their neighbours acquiring the latest U.S. weaponry, especially those for whom violent border disputes are still a reality or a recent memory. Peru and Ecuador fought a bloody jungle border war only last year, Venezuela and Colombia and Central American neighbours like Honduras and El Salvador have tension on their borders, and Argentina nearly went to war with Chile in 1978.

Argentine Defence Minister Jorge Dominguez, hosting talks which follow a first regional defence summit in Williamsburg, Virginia, in July last year, asked Perry on Monday "to keep an arms balance in the region," Argentine officials said.

The Argentine military, which has seen its own budget shrink rapidly under the government of President Carlos Menem and which has agreed with its giant neighbour Brazil not to increase military spending, is particularly concerned about Chile's interest in buying U.S. F-16 fighters.

Washington wants calm such fears by proposing the advance notification of "significant weapons purchases. This is another openness measure, confidence building through transparency," said Perry. "Countries tend to make worse case estimates of what their neighbours are doing in the absence of openness."

Perry said he would use the Bariloche talks to announce a U.S. plan to establish a U.S.-based Inter-American Centre for Defence Studies, aimed at training civilians "to more effectively control military matters."
He also planned to express U.S. support for Panama's proposal to be the base for a multi-national centre to fight narco-trafficking, possibly with links to Howard Air Base in the United States.

"Panama is located right on the edge of some of the most substantial narco-trafficking problems that exist anywhere in the hemisphere," said Perry. "One of the greatest difficulties in dealing with and fighting the narcotics traffic is that each nation deals with this problem as a national problem. But narcotic trafficking is international in nature, it does not respect borders."
